findings.title: Dead fallback in FollowUp.Key() for an error json.Marshal cannot produce
findings.detail: Key() marshals a []any of only strings, ints and nil (see lines 90-97); json.Marshal cannot fail for those types (it only errors on channels, funcs, complex numbers, cyclic references or unsupported types), and the comment at lines 100-102 says as much ("Unreachable"). The fmt.Sprintf("%v", parts) fallback is therefore a legacy-style defensive branch that can never execute — a dead fallback per the over-engineering rubric (item 4). Not harmful, but it adds a branch and an unreachable format-based key-rendering path that will never be exercised by any test. Low priority: could simply be `b, _ := json.Marshal(parts); return string(b)` with a one-line comment noting why the error is ignored.

findings.title: alignmentVerdictLine grows unrequested unknown-verdict handling
findings.detail: Task 4's brief specifies alignmentLine's four cases (skipped / awaiting confirmation / confirmed-pending-verdicts / today's counts line) but says nothing about handling verdict words outside alignmentVerdictOrder. The diff adds a `seen` map plus a second pass that collects and sort.Strings' any unrecognised verdict word into a `rest` bucket (lines 616-633) — extra state and a second loop to defend against an auditor emitting a word the fixed order doesn't know. It's a reasonable robustness fix (previously such words were silently dropped) but it is scope creep beyond what the task asked for in a diff whose other status changes are otherwise minimal and tightly scoped to the brief. Flagging for awareness rather than blocking — the added complexity is small and self-contained.
